cards.question: What is the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary triage?
cards.answer: Primary triage at scene now uses NARU Ten Second Triage (walking, severe bleeding, talking, penetrating torso injury) to assign P1/P2/P3/Not Breathing, with life-saving bleeding control and airway positioning done during triage. Secondary triage at the casualty clearing station uses the NHS Major Incident Triage Tool (MITT), which replaced the Triage Sieve and Triage Sort in 2023. Tertiary triage occurs in hospital after initial resuscitation and continuously thereafter.

cards.question: What are the principles of damage-control resuscitation?
cards.answer: Rapid source control, restrictive resuscitation with SBP 80–90 mmHg only when there is no brain injury, early protocol-based blood products, TXA, ionised-calcium monitoring and warming. European 2023 guidance specifies TXA 1 g over 10 minutes within 3 hours then 1 g over 8 hours; severe TBI requires MAP ≥80 mmHg rather than permissive hypotension. Adapt to the applicable local protocol.

cards.question: How are nerve-agent (organophosphate) casualties managed?
cards.answer: Protect responders and prevent secondary contamination. Disrobe and use appropriate decontamination while trained, protected teams provide urgent resuscitation and antidotes. Treat respiratory secretions and circulatory toxicity with atropine, give pralidoxime and treat convulsions with benzodiazepines according to current TOXBASE/specialist advice. Pupils are not an atropine endpoint. Support ventilation and avoid suxamethonium because paralysis may be prolonged.
